title: e-scape: digital business incubators for social regeneration
author: Jennifer Brown
description: This study examined the urban infrastructure and workplace needs of technology start-up companies.
findings: Categorised business incubators into the following types: community, commerical, innovation, internet, live work. These differ in their relationships with the startup, for example internet incubators provide cheap support packages which can be provided via the internet whereas innovation incubators are larger companies which invite small start-ups into their offices to exchange business expertise for innovation.
outputs: This research contributed to Tower Hamlets regeneration strategy, in particular to proposals for the site of Poplar Baths.
partner: Gestetner in a consortium with Geoffrey Reid Associates, GMW Partnership, Jones Lang LaSalle, Peabody Trust and Roneo Office Systems

title: Cities in the shade: sustainable urban lighting in the public realm
author: Megan Charnley
description: This study investigated shifts in trends and concerns in urban lighting and sought to discover a way of balancing energy efficiency with a sense of identity.
findings: Discovered a shift in concerns in urban lighting from crime prevention and wayfinding to developing a sense of urban identity to benefit the people who live in the areas being lit.
outputs: The Nighttime Neighbourhood Network lighting strategy of brightly-lit nodes. A working prototype of TubeLite. A strip light within a steel tube mount, used to construct illuminated goal posts on a local football pitch.
challenges: lack of overlap between the research and product design phases meant it was difficult to evaluate what the original participating community groups thought of the goal posts
partner: Megaman Charity Trust Fund and Paviom

title: Metricity: Exploring new measures of urban density
author: Paul Clarke
description: This study examined current national and local policy guidelines which define the density levels prescribed to urban and inner city development in order to provide discourse about how to plan, define and measure the density metric of sustainable communities.
findings: Uncovered a growing shift of employment density towards the Central Business District, establishing a greater mono-centric city as declining outer London office space and increased office development in central London has created a greater reliance on mobility to reach employment opportunities.
outputs: Devised four density principles for investigating the policy contribution of different factors in relation to user need: intensity (mixed-use density), amenity (typological denisty), autonomy (density of inhabitation), frequency (density of interaction).
challenges: confidentiality issues and continuous workload stream of individuals involved in the case study live-project restricted their ability to contribute to the research
partner: 3D Reid, Arup, British Council for Offices, Child Graddon Lewis, Fletcher Priest Trust, UrbanBuzz

title: Blighted landscapes: the narrative role of street lighting in urban regeneration
author: Matthew Dearlove
description: This study sets out a design framework for Tower Hamlets to develop its own identity and environment and suggests ways in which Targetti can engage with public housing and public space so that street lighting plays a narrative role in urban regeneration.
findings: Around observed sites there was unused space which had become a meeting point for drinking, drug-use, etc. while none of the community organisations shared communal space for acitivities and seemed to lack communication. Interviews revealed that the key issues to be resolved were security, disruptive and anti-social behaviour, stairwells, corridors and dark corners, relationship between street and estate, access across estate, lighting, green areas, play areas for children and communal seating.
outputs: Produced a site strategy for St Peters Square involving a public strip separated by a wall providing a lit screen, message box, private allotments and a football pitch/cinema.

title: Light.urban.landscape: Lighting strategies for regenerating the city
author: Harry Dobbs
description: This study looked at the role of public lighting in regenerating complex urban areas in order to develop a set of guidelines on how to approach urban lighting with consideration given to the wider cultural context of the city.
findings: Uncovered a complex range of issues and agendas that are inherent within our central urban fabric which illustated the need for a coherent approach with which to handle them.
outputs: A set of guidelines for lighting to support urban regeneration, divided into marketing, art and landscape phases to inform Targetti's development and marketing of products and services as well as action for any local authority engaged in urban regeneration.

title: Food for thought: a service-based approach for embedding innovation
author: Re Dubhthaigh; Toke Barter
description: This project explored the role of innovation in corporate organisations, to 'demystify' innovation practice and create, through a service-based approach, a framework for embedding innovation tools and processes into everyday working life.
findings: Innovation is encouraged but not supported by businesses. Most innovation models invite short, external injections of fresh ideas and much of the knowledge gained at these events is lost when everyday work routines begin again. Innovation processes and tools often lack a guiding framework within organisations. Using external innovation consultants leads to a perceived loss of project ownership by internal teams. Innovation is misrepresented as a moment of magical or divine inspiration leading to the belief that the process of innovation is only available to the 'gifted few'. New kinds of working environments are often under-utilised due to organisational mindsets.
outputs: Proposition of an in-house, cross-organisational innovation support service with a framework that is analogous to the service structure of a restaurant, offering 'Innovation Snacking', 'Fast Food Innovation', 'Gourmet Innovation' with 'the chef' providing leadership at a strategic level, 'the cooks' forming a creative production team and 'the waiters' liasing between different groups.

title: Light Volumes, Dark Matters: patterns for sustainable lighting
author: Claudia Dutson
description: This project considered how light can be used in office buildings to support the health and productivity of workers and to increase energy efficiency.
findings: Discovered the main problems workers have with light in offices are too much brightness, not enough natural light, too dark, unchanging or fluorescent lighting all day.
outputs: Model of a tower inside which visitors can change the lighting by removing or adding walls to serve as a research tool in workshops.

title: Glowing Places: interactive lighting for large public interiors
author: Megumi Fujikawa
description: This project explored innovative ways for people to interact with light in public space and demonstrated the role of lighting in signifying changing emotional states.
findings: Most people interviewed had negative or no impression of the interior lighting condition of a shopping centre but have a positive response to the ambiguous lighting pulse of a light ball and associate it with their body.
outputs: A chair that glows with different intensities depending on how long people sit on it to be placed around shopping centres.

title: Aging in a vertical city
author: Gheerawo, Rama
description: This project explored the delights, challenges and frustrations of aging in Hong Kong.
findings: Bed spaces in carehomes and homes with elderly people in Hong Kong are often shared by several people and typically have a colour palette relating to hospitals rather than homes (mostly grey, brown bed frame, green-yellow curtain). Food delivery to care homes poses several difficulties such as no meal delivery services in the morning or on Sundays and older people being unable to choose mealtimes to match their daily routines.
outputs: Several design ideas. Specifically, a bed space with a darker, enclosed space for sleeping and open, lighter space for other activities; a bed unit on wheels; a bed space which makes more effective use of colour, e.g. uses different colours to mark out different areas, uses graduations of colour instead of solid blocks; an Artificial Intelligence which helps to look after personal diet by assessing learning and giving advice on what to eat; tableware which is adapted for use by elderly people e.g. a bowl which is landscaped at the bottom, a tray with increased friction.
website: Observation, Interviews, Scenarios, Prototyping, Immersive Research, Workshops

title: Creative Citizens
author: Catherine Greene; Dan Lockton
description: This project investigated how the tools and techniques of the creative economy are being used to build new community networks and innovative forms of civic life. One strand examined the development of hyperlocal media across the UK to investigate the role of community journalism in holding local power to account and giving citizens a voice. Another strand sought to understand the value of community-led design as a type of creative citizenship and how media can support or transform this practice. A third strand explored how 'South Blessed', an informal youth network of creative citizens, generated value through its activities and a fourth explored how professional creative citizenship and its related network was embodied through 'the Moseley Exchange' a co-working space, and how it overlaped with other types of creative citizenship in Moseley.
findings: Both audience and producer play a creative citizenship role in hyperlocal news although local citizens are not always being effectively engaged by their hyperlocal organisations' choice of approach. Most communities require support to benefit from access to media tools. Participation in creative community projects fuels participants sense of public voice and drive to contribute to a wider shared culture. Creative citizenship cannot be classed as an uncontested unified body as enactments of creativitiy and citizenship are diverse and there can even exist tensions between different (e.g. social and environmental) objectives.
outputs: The Creative Citizens Conference, held in 2014. Indigo Babies, a 32 page comic that tells the story of a group of inner city youth with superhuman talents and special techno powers caught up in having to make moral choices during a moment of community insurrection. Crown Root Publications, a self-publishing arm. Creative Citizens' Variety Pack, a collection of 12 inspirational community projects, all making use of digital tools in creative ways for social benefit, with practical suggestions and advice.

title: Totalscape: work/live business incubators for the creative industries
author: Yan Ki Lee
description: This project developed a framework for understanding the living requirements for those running a creative business from home and applied this framework to developing a design proposal which aims to meet these requirements.
findings: There are stages in the development of the relationship between the work/live space and business growth: workspace mixes with home, workspace spreads over home, workspace separates from home and consideration should be given to ways of facilitating a smooth transition from the first to the third stage.
outputs: Totalscape, an alternative campus-scale design proposal involving three levels: work/live components, community and campus.
partner: Peabody Trust in a consortium with Geoffrey Reid Associates, GMW Partnership, Jones Lang LaSalle, Gestetner and Roneo Office Systems

title: Wandervogel: involving the local community in on-street digital networks
author: Indri Tulusan
description: This project developed interactive content for an on-street digital information system with the aim of engaging local communities.
outputs: Culture Cloud, a map of location-based blogs hosted by local residents or community groups.
challenges: Cityspace raised concern about legal issues relating to content being unfiltered

title: The heart friendly office: a communication tool for architects and designers
author: Mike Bond; Martin Coyne
description: This project looks at ways in which workplace designers can help reduce levels of heart disease in the UK in order to produce a web-based information tool aimed at promoting healthier practice in office design.
findings: The major factors in the workplace that contribute to Coronary Heart Disease are stress, temperature, attitudes to stairs, location of car park, shift work, ergonomics and hydration.
outputs: Heart Friendly Office, a communication channel with an internet-ased information set comprising a Healoth Information Databse, Best Practice Case Studies and Feedback Advice.

title: Pluspoint: an auto-injector system for anaphylaxis attack
author: Jamie Cobb
description: This project summarises the concept of an automatic adrenaline administering technology to help those that experience allergic reactions
findings: Many poeple, particularaly younger children struggle with administering adrenaline auto-injectors. Prohibitive size, trauma experiance, poor labelling are all problems with the current auto injectors (epipen and anapen).
outputs: Design and Development of Pluspoint, an improved adrenaline auto injector that is both significantly smaller and more intuitive to use, developed to the point of Initial Prototypes and IP protection.

title: Ambulance Design for Patient Safety: towards a national ambulance fleet Future ambulances
author: Roger Coleman; Dale Harrow; Evans Owen; Merih Kunur; Sally Halls
description: This project investigates the developing needs of service provision and the short and long term requirements of vehicles and equipment that will be needed to address the concerns of patient and staff safety in the future in the Ambulance Service and recommends primary considerations for emergency care vehicles and equipment.
findings: Discovered that there is a lack of consistency in ambulance design which reduces efficiency but a strong desire for standardisation in design of ambulances and that the composition of ambulance fleets is changing due to improved response systems, increased care and provision of a wider range of services, leading to a requirement for three core vehicle types.
outputs: Identified nine design challenges and expanded these into a series of performance requirements and established a three stage design direction and design ideas for the core vehicles.
challenges: there was a divergence between the National Reporting and Learning System data and the incidents reported by individual trusts used by researchers to provide the framework for workshop discussion

title: Reading the signs: wayfinding for dementia
author: Lottie Crumbleholme
description: This study looks at how residents living with dementia find their way around in Bupa care homes and makes recommendations for improving signage.
findings: Signage should not be thought about in isolation but in the context of its environment including considering aspects of interior design as well as what life is like in the homes day to day.
outputs: A set of guidelines for designing carehomes to support residents living with dementia in finding their way around.

title: Design bugs out: improving patient safety on hospital wards
author: Grace Davey
description: This project brought designers together with clinical specialists, patients and frontline staff to make hospital furniture and equipment easier and quicker to clean to help control the risk of healthcare associated infections.
outputs: Several hospital furniture prototypes which were showcased at key healthcare events and at seven NHS hospitals.
partner: Design Council, NHS Purchasing and Supply Agency, Department of Health

title: Redesigning the ambulance: improving mobile emergency healthcare
author: Gianpaolo Fusari; Yusuf Muhammad
description: This project builds on existing evidence and previous work to redesign the interior of the modern emergency ambulance.
findings: In the original design, the side loader concept was the least popular modification and least likely to succeed and the repositioning of the stretcher into the middle of the vehicle was the most popular. In the second design the most popular modifications were the introduction of a bariatric stretcher and moving and handling equipment in the same cupboard accessible from inside and outside the vehicle.
outputs: A final prototype of an ambulance interior for testing and feedback before building and road testing the new ambulance.

title: Resus:station: redesign of the resuscitation trolley
author: Sally Halls; Jonathan West
description: This project reconsidered the design of the resusitation trolley, in order to promote faster and more efficient treatment.
findings: A large number of design triggers generated from shortcomings that clinicians treat as 'a fact of life'. Co-design took these ideas further with 4 main functions: of splitting, storage, resusitation, and restocking.
outputs: Final Prototype for redesigned station, with direct feedback from users, ready for the next design iteration.

title: Body 2.0: extending ability through 3D printed technology
author: Jordan Jon Hodgson
description: This project considered how people could extend their ability by looking at the possibilities presented by the emerging field of low cost open source 3D printed prosthetics. The research aimed to focus upon the emotional context relating to the look and feel of the prosthetics as opposed to the mechatronic success of the function.
findings: Participants were excited by the opportunity to express their personalities through a bespoke limb including through tattoos.
outputs: Several 3D printed prosthetic test models.

title: Redesigning surgical tools: disposable primary cut instruments Cutting Edge
author: Maja Kecman; Lisa Storux
description: This project details the design and devleopment of 2 new sergical tool concepts for knee surger
findings: Many current tools are expensive and difficult to use, making surgery longer and therefore more dangerous for patients. Surgeons are often picky with the tools and equpment they chose to use, they often prioritise tools that make them feel comfortable and accurate, aiming to improve how effectively they can work.
outputs: Two design proposals that were iteratively taken back to surgeons and other users for development, before undergoing direct use case testing.

title: Stepping stone: designing an inclusive pedometer
author: Barry Menmuir
description: This project describes the research and development of a low-cost step ocunter for use by participants, especially older people, in the Walking The Way To Health Initiative.
findings: 95% of walkers did not use a pedometer and current pedometers are not attractive to customers, feeling scientific or technical.
outputs: Single design concept for a redesigned pedometer, including CAD and physical 3D printed models

title: Support system: empowering people with osteoarthritis
author: Ela Neagu; Lizzie Raby
description: This project describes the creation of a digital 'hub' or portal for those with osteoarthritis to be able to share their experiences and advice. Later focussing on the needs of recently diagnoesd people and how they can receive encouragment and support.
findings: Current support systems and doctors don't provide the advice and information that is important for someone living out their life with these conditions. Particularly for the recently diagnosed, there isn't a positive resource or self-help guidance.
outputs: A proposal for a platform that allows people to share their experience and advice for living with arthritis. The ARUK 'Challenge' is also proposed: a social media campaign that encourages people to post and engage about their experience, and promotes ways to improve muskuloskeletal health.

title: Impact wave: developing clothing that cares and protects
author: Dan Plant
description: This project developed a system of flexible body armour combining wearability with human protection.
findings: Currently available body impact protection is limited because it is either based upon a rigid exterior shell, which is inflexible and uncomfortable, or a foam laminate, which inhibits performance.
outputs: An Active Protection System which protects the human body from abrasions and impacts, made from a strain rate sensitive polymer which reacts to impact and a flexible outer sheath of Hytrel.
challenges: product unable to progress immediately towards entering the marketplace due to need to pass health and safety tests, expense of the mouldings and limited budget
partner: Levi Strauss Europe, Middle East and Africa

title: Foot print: a campaign for walking the way to health
author: Eleanor Ridsdale
description: This study looked at ways in which communication materials such as posters and maps can encourage people at risk from heart disease to join local walking groups and exercise regularly.
targetedUser: people at risk from heart disease
findings: Posters should include the statement 'everyone needs 30 minutes walking 5 days a week at a moderate pace' and the location of posters important.
outputs: Posters to encourage walking instead getting the bus or a lift or escalator and maps showing a route for led and independent walks in Keighley.

title: Healthy pregnancy: redefining the experience (woven stories)
author: Florrie Salnot
description: This study explored the experiences of pregnant women and implemented the research through design solutions to help women get better social support.
findings: due to change of life, risk of miscarriage, lack of medical support and intense discomforts, the first trimester of pregnancy is the most difficult for a majority of women
outputs: Woven-stories, a website which enables women to record their experiences of pregnancy and weaves them together to offer advice and information to other pregnant women

title: Graphic Guidance, information design for patient safety
author: Thea Swayne
description: This project helped to establish a benchmark in good design for the packaging of medicine.
outputs: A fully illustrated set of design considerations with both good and bad examples and recommendations for design of secondary packaging including dispensing label and faces of the packaging and of primary packaging specifically a blister strip.

title: Design for Dementia: improving the care home environment for people with dementia
author: Gregor Timlin; Nic Rysenbry
description: This project explores how better product and environmental design can improve quality of life for carehome patients with dementia.
findings: Cognitive ability is improved by promoting the use of familiar and recognisable surroundings and activities that respond to resigents' deepest and earliest memories. Social ability is addressed through the design of artefacts and aqmenities that create opportunities for residents and staff to interact more easily in activities of daily living. Physical ability is promoted through design which unobtrusively compensates for disabilities such as mobility and vision which are prevalent among care home residents.
outputs: Recommendations for the layout of dining areas and bedrooms and design ideas including a range of tableware.
challenges: had to create research methods which were sensitive to the needs of and respectful towards people with dementia

title: web-based platform to allow surgeons to go through pre-oparative processes
author: Hawys Tomos
description: Investigate the wider surgical landscape and attiudes of surgeons focusing on surgical process to achieve better patient outcomes. improve geometry of knee replacement - make things 'tailored' to both the surgeon and the patient
findings: Patient specific operations are ideal (knee geometry), but infeasable due to cost.
outputs: Concepts such as a tablet app platform to allow surgeons to input their limits and visualise surgical processes, as well as a long-leg assesment tool and a jig designed to aid tibial resection.

title: Circles of Care
author: Indri Tulusan
description: This project investigates the different strategies and experiences of users building their own social networks of health and proposes a complimentary healthcare model or landscape where user strategies and experiences can be supported.
targetedUser: network providers, retailers and medical product companies, voluntary sector organisations, the NHS
findings: People create their own self-care strategies and increasingly rely on personal support networks before or after going to the doctor. People have circles of care but are often not aware of them.
outputs: A map of the space inbetween self help and expert medical help which shows how we build, adapt, share and pass on our personal health network with key life stages mapped against health needs and opportunities for developing social networks to address them supported by scenarios suggesting new service opportunities linking private, public and voluntary sector organisations in new partnerships.

title: Kinder: quality time at the work-station
author: Pascal Anson
description: This project examines the implications of working for long periods at a desk with a Personal Computer on it.
findings: The following key questions from the office workers emerged: Should I be sitting like this? Can I work and eat properly at the same time? Is my stuff safe? Take a break or carry on tired? Where is the nature, all I see is plastic?
outputs: Mini' series of office furniture including mini table, mini garden, mini bed.

title: Family rituals: keeping mobile workers connected
author: Jo-Anne Bichard; David Chatting
description: This project investigates the ritual activities that families engage in during periods of remote working and speculates on the potential roles of technology in mediating complex working family lives.
findings: Organisations did not consider the needs of mobile workers beyond what was required to perform their jobs. The activity most important to most families was eating and drinking including shopping for food and preparation. Families with younger children had rituals associated with their children like bedtime stories. Ability to connect is often limited by time. Relationships found to be maintainable in some ways at a distance through digital technology.
outputs: Ritual Machine 1, a beer bottle opener connected to the internet which when used in any location pours a glass of wine at home. Ritual Machine 2, a flip-dot display connected to an iPhone app via which users can connect with the display. Ritual Machine 3, a robot vacuum cleaner which vacuums in response to the movements of the absent family member. Ritual Machine 4, a jam jar which can be spoken into a replays messages to the absent family member. Ritual Machine 5, an electronic telescope that can be pointed in any direction and shows an illustrated depiction of part of the world and another device which the absent family member can take with them to leave a marker at the correct place in the illustrated world.
challenges: to recruit mobile workers and their families forced to use a lot of different approaches to generate interest, design ethnographies challenging as families reluctant to allow additional investigation to interrupt private family time
partner: Newcastle University, University of West of England, Bournemouth University

title: Work well: Inclusive furniture for older office workers
author: Jeremy Gay
description: This project found and illustrated areas of opportunity in the design of work furniture for older users and developed inclusive new concepts as exemplars that address the specific needs and desires of an ageing workforce.
findings: Older workers often feel unable to change aspects of their immediate environment that are important to them, are made victims of simple usability problems, fail to use work furniture properly and maintain good work habits, are more likely to hot desk, often work outside the office in places with inadequate facilities, are adopting more mobile working habits that can have adverse consquences on their health and well-being, are interested in health issues and open to innovation in this area, are hindered in the adoption of more healthy working habits by lack of provision of amenities, see sharing knowledge as one of the key ways to connect with people in the workplace.
outputs: CASTRO, a meeting table for up to five people that allows greater control over the immediate environment. AQUA, a translucent screen system for acoustic and visual control in open plan work settings. STRETCH, a series of stacking chairs that visually prompt more active working habits. NEMES, an under-desk pedestal for user customisation in hot-desking settings. HEMET, a furniture unit which supports offers working facilities for public spaces. MOTORO, a micro workstation and travel case. PRESENCE, a device for use with any task chair providing proactive healthcare information at work through simple user sensing abilities. ASAS, a circular, modular seating system for adding a multi-functional amenity area to space-restricted workplaces. PLATO, a multi-functional concept for temporary learning and teamwork settings.

title: Space for thought: designing for knowledge workers
author: Catherine Greene
description: This study explores the ways in which workspaces can be designed to support knowledge workers.
findings: Knowledge workers desire comfort, an adaptable desk, lack of distractions, flexible project furniture, a welcoming environment, control over environment and alternative workspaces.
outputs: AcousticWorks (a mobile acoustic screen), Adaptable Table (a table divider that can be raised up to provide a whiteboard), GardenWorks (a modular screen to provide a visual barriar), Flexible Project Furniture, Suspended Room (suspended curtains), Luxury Hot-desking, Digital Portal (a facility for making video conferencing calls), Kitchen as Meeting Room, Digital Messageboard (a means of communicating to one's desk your current location and when you will return)

title: Places please: a temporary environment to enhance team working
author: Greg Epps
description: This project resulted in the development of a component based system capable of temporarily transforming space to enhance the collaborative experience and enable organisations to innovate more effectively.
outputs: Developed a strategy for the documentation of team behaviour in the workplace, a system of architectural components, including a 'portal', 'props trolly' and 'tablet', and a new set of scenarios which illustrated a transformed and heightened team experience.

title: Home-Work: rethinking home office furniture
author: Peter Fullagar; Dan Jones
description: This project examined home office furniture from the user's perspective and developed a range of home office furniture in response to this.
findings: Classified the needs of home workers into physical, psychological and social and existing home office furniture into single boundary, dual boundary crossover and fully integrated solutions and discovered that none of the commerically available furniture types fit within the fully integrated solution.
outputs: The Envelope Desk, a desk with two levels with a wood finish on the outside to integrate the desk into the home and a plain inside surface and strip light to simulate an office environment.

title: Capture it: a future workplace for the multi-generational knowledge worker
author: Harriet Harriss; Suzi Winstanley
description: This project explored what is meant by 'knowledge' in the context of the multi-generational workplace and proposed possible designs for workplaces that respond to the likely nature of the future workforce.
findings: Older workers demand more choice and control over how they work, are increasingly curious and committed to learning, require space and time for reflection, look to multi-sensory work environments especially green spaces to support their work, increasingly recognise a fundamental relationship between tactile materials and cognitive abilities, want access to new technology, have a need for triggers in the environment to facilitate narrative and memory and crave connection to people of all ages.
outputs: SHARE, a team space for sharing knowledge between people of diverse ages. TRADE, an oral database of generations of knowledge. FOCUS, a marketplace to trade knowledge between organisations. REFLECT, a series of screens for focusing on individual work. CONNECT, a digital network to link the knowledge of a diverse workforce.

title: Working Light (Office Lighting for an ageing workforce) Lighten Up: Office Lighting for Future Work Patterns and an Aging Workforce?
author: Harrison, Matthew
description: This study examines the ways in which the office enviornment can be improved through lighting design to encourage people to remain in work as they get older.
findings: Discovered the key areas of innovation to be light for health, light for communication and envioronmental and natural light.

title: Flexible workers/fluid workscape: supporting work-life balance
author: Ian Johnston
description: This study examines the behaviour and characteristics of an increasingly mobile group of senior office workers.
findings: Flexible work patterns are leading to an extension of the working week and to the traditional boundaries between work and leisure breaking down with people working in places traditionally associated with leisure such as pubs and cafes.
outputs: Product ideas including skateboard briefcase, work bags, work suits, pen/clock, interactive diary.

title: Off the wall: organising the transferable workplace
author: Arash Kaynama
description: This study sought to design new office products to support the shift towards taking work and office products home.
findings: Divided working personality traits into organised, individual, particular, flexible and mobile, each of which would benefit from a different sort of product.
outputs: The shaker office (hook system to hold files etc), tetris office (storage system of interlocking shapes), missing office (pegboard system), magnetic office (work tools that are magnetic and glow in the dark), moving office (transforming briefcase).

title: Shared space: enhancing social dynamics in office building
author: Kirsteen Mackay
description: This study examines new architectural strategies to enhance social dynamics in office buildings, with a focus on the manipulation of various shared spaces with the potential to enhance social dynamics.
findings: Identified four 'communities of scale' which illustrate different types of social dynamic in different building and organisational types: Magnet (national industry sector), Matrix (global organisation), Mentor (within a group), Mutual (across rank). The ways in which shared spaces can be manipulated to enhance social dynamics include introduction of a social core in office buildings, in-house business incubators, foyers and cellular offices for use by anyone.
outputs: Guidance for how to introduce changes to the design of offices including introducing a research phase into the initial building process, opening and maintaining a conversation with those who will be using the space and paying attention to work methodology and environment.

title: Office-less office: paper-like displays for home working
author: Eddie Mundy
description: This project envisioned uses for paper-like electronic display technologies in a range of social contexts, developing a series of design artefacts to communicate potential and identify user applications.
findings: The practical nature of the work and its emphasis on things happening outside the home hinder attempts by those working from home to use technology.
outputs: Confidential catalgoue for HP Labs which explores new product applications, design proposals for home workers of digital work pads and tools which are similar to pen and pape. A focused design research study simulating new tools for home workers shown at the RCA in 2001.
challenges: the technologies were still under development during the testing phase so the user group were not able to try the products, only to 'experience' them through explanations of their functions and 'walking through' scenarios for use

title: Workplace and wellbeing: what aspects of workplace design are most important to people’s wellbeing
author: Jeremy Myerson; Gail Ramster; Andrew Thomson
description: This study explored which aspects of workplace design are perceived by employees to be important to wellbeing and whether giving greater participation in the design of the workplace environment increases the sense of control and welllbeing of people at work.
findings: There is constant change in the workplace with the majority of changes being perceived by users to be for the benefit of the organisation at their expense and without taking their functional and psychological needs into account. Wellbeing supported by connection to outside, variety of spaces, control over space, particiption in design process.
outputs: A conceptual model to chart and assess wellbeing needs in the workplace with two axes of need (functional to psychological, organisation to individual).

title: Workplace and wellbeing: developing a practical framework for workplace design to affect employee wellbeing
author: Jeremy Myerson; Catherine Greene; Imogen Privett; Gail Ramster; Andrew Thomson
description: This study resulted in the development of a practical tool to help companies use workplace design to affect and improve employees wellbeing.
findings: Those engaged in the Participatory Design Project registered a higher increase in their mental wellbeing than the team not invited to participate and the solutions given were those that gave them greater control over and ownership of their workspace.
outputs: An evaluation toolkit which uses information from the workers to create an overall picture of how well the organisation is meeting their psychological and functional needs which employees can use to generate ideas for making improvements in the workplace to support their wellbeing.
partner: Gensler, Bupa, Kinnarps, Milliken and Shell

title: Head space: privacy in open plan offices
author: Tim Parsons
description: This study explored ways to provide open-plan office workers with increased levels of privacy through the design of objects used on and around the desk.
findings: Solutions which involve the use of recognisable objects and those which invite participation and creative use are most successful.
outputs: Umbrella chair, desk post box, 'no door' mat, phone tone recognition system using light, washing line screen, phone and e-mail hut, work in progress rack.

title: Living Stages: what can workplaces learn from theatre design
author: Imogen Privett
description: This study examines the potential of theatrical effects, specifically lighting, tanslucency and colour, to enhance the performance of work tasks in an open-plan office environment.
outputs: Created a vocabulary of elements (vista, levels, colour, screens, projection and effects, light and shadow) inspired by stage design to provide a new framework for office designers and the clients to think about the psychological wellbeing of the workforce as well as their physical comfort.

title: Playground: inclusive design for disabled homeworkers
author: Lotta Vaananen
description: This project uncovered the challenges faced by people with disabilities who use IT to work from home and developed products to improve their productivity, well-being and quality of life.
findings: Several participants did not have a specially designed working area and many of those who did shared it with someone else.
outputs: The Carousel, horse shoe-shaped table and swivelling platform to allow the wheelchair to function as any office chair. The Swing, reclining chair for work.
challenges: concern over promoting home working for disabled people at the expense of encouraging increased accessibility in offices

title: The abilizer: aiding rehabilitation for disabled people
author: Judith Anderson
description: This project follows the research and development (from concept to manufacture) of a wheelchair-mounted support system, which enables users to stand and balance in social situations.
findings: There are important clinical reasons for being able to stand as well as the social impact. Further feasibility of a device that allows wheelchair users to engage in standing was analysed but there were manufacturing and implimentation issues.
outputs: Three iterative prototypes of the Abilizer concept were produced and tested with users.
challenges: Financial difficulties meant that the final 3rd prototype was unable to be manufactured, meaning key features were missing for some user testing.

title: Urban moving 2030 transport typologies for the future
author: Shaun Hutchinson
description: This study imagines the future of personal vehicles based on ideas of autonomous technology, mobility on demand, and handheld connectivity devices to engage with communal mobility vehicles.
findings: Established four mobility categories:  commuting, entertainment seeking, dwelling, area visiting.
outputs: Each with their own vehicle archetype and adaptations, serving purposes from customised driverless last mile transport to driving for entertainment.

title: Keep driving safely: a campaign for older drivers
author: Paul John-Baptiste
description: This project indentifies and addresses key issues with driving for an older demographic, and moves to create an informative campaign to directly affect road users.
findings: Older people suffer more seriously from road accidents, and aren't adressed by current media campaigns for safe driving. This means factors like giving up driving aren't addressed.
outputs: Communication campaign - series of posters/ads targeted at older drivers, as well as a distribution plan for the campain to be able to target the older user base.

title: Urban Flow: mapping inclusive transport
author: Helen Jones
description: This study explored the potential for inclusive and integrated design strategies to inform future urban transport soluctions and identifies a need for new design briefing tools to create a bridge between social reserach into cities and design for moblitliy.
targetedUser: All public transport users and potential public transport users, young transport designers
findings: Identified issues with rapidly changing urban centres, and mobility systems are under increasing pressure. Despite this, transport designers often do not consider the social/cultral/demographic trends in these areas.
outputs: interviews and other data were presented to government in the Design Council policy paper. The Design Breifing map is a tool to encourage transport designers to use mapping to ensure wider requirements and considerations throughout a project. Initiatives were planned to communicate the ideas found in the study to vehicle design students at the RCA.

title: Mobilicity: scenarios for sustainable public transport 2025
author: Merih Kunur
description: This project explores new directions in sustainable mass transit for commuters and residents in the increasingly crowded urban environment.
findings: London, Istanbul and Hong Kong investigated as examples of polycentric cities with transport operating on fixed routes. Due to this transport vehicles should be flexible, adaptable and allow express services to enhance travel times.
outputs: A single design concept for a modular mass transit vehicle, incorporating adaptable routing concepts identified through each city case study.

title: TH!NK Connected car: sustainable and inclusive mobility.
author: Filip Krnja
description: This study imagines the future of the car, specifically in the connected car concept, making vehicles more communicative and intelligent.
findings: Connectivity, Privacy, Interface found to be the areas where people have greatest issues with the design of cars.
outputs: User research personas were complied and published on the internet. The three main areas were ideated on and implemented into a single vehicle design concept.
partner: Norwegian Design Council through the IT Funk Programme and Research Council of Norway

title: How people do it: taking young children on public transport in London.
author: Marie Lenclos
description: This project aimed to research and communicate the problems with London’s public transport system, for those who have young children.
targetedUser: young parents, users of TFL netowork
findings: Despite progress in making TFL public transport more accessable, many young parents struggle travelling with children. They often opt to walk or drive, despite speed or cost benefits of using public transport.
outputs: Informative/documentary film showcasing the struggles and expeiences of young parents travelling with their children on London's public transport network.
partner: Geoffrey Reid Associates and Transport for London

title: Info-motion adapting the car cockpit to future needs
author: Serge Porcher
description: This project explores technologies to redesign the automotive dashboard, investigating interactive/dynamic projections and displays as a progression from standard readouts and physical interface.
findings: Future driving needs are more diverse and more dense with information than the current cockpits were able to provide for.
outputs: Final concept of a dashboard is created, which provides a large interaction surface, where information can be changed depending on the vehicle's context at any moment in time.

title: Tilting Trike: a pedal vehicle for all abilities
author: Ben Wilson
description: This report describes the research and development of a new pedal powered tricycle for children that can be quickly adapted to the needs of those without lower body strength.
targetedUser: young people without lower body strength, all young people
findings: Identified and developed a concept for a pedal vehicle that is both desirable and accessable. Identifying customisability and ease of modification as key features that allow users to better fit the trike to their individual needs and abilities.
outputs: Two final prototype trikes were produced, setup in both pedal powered and hand powered configurations. These prototypes were also designed with manufacture in mind, using standard methods and components.

title: Process to pleasure: instinctive wayfinding at Heathrow airport
author: Karen Adcock; Carl Turner
description: This study propses a new 'sensory landscape'' within Heathrow Terminal 5, which aims to make the scale of the building more human and manageable for all ages and abilities.
findings: Series of design proposals developed to help both users and staff to 'manage the scale of the building'. Mapping of sensory landscape. The primary issues identified were: creating sense of location within space, engagement with space in non-functional cases, assisting wayfinding. Though generated through special needs analysis, these were applicable to all.
outputs: Several concepts created to tackle issues with information display and information arch idea taken forward for further development.

title: Process to pleasure: instinctive wayfinding at Heathrow airport
author: Karen Adcock; Carl Turner
description: This report describes the second of a 3 year study into inclusive design principles within Heathrow Terminal 5. It details the development of concepts formed in the first year, and prepares them for testing and evaluation within the existing Heathrow Terminal 1.
findings: Instinctive wayfinding and communication design. After establishing the site for the trial, devleopment of ways of communicating the information specific to that site were discussed.
outputs: Development of a proposal for an 'information gate' at the the T1/T2 junction, with an emphasis on communicating wayfinding and passenger routing. Many communication techniques were used including colour coding, as well as other senosry elements to help prepare passengers.

title: Process to pleasure: wayfinding principles for the airport terminal
author: Samson Adjei; Pascal Anson
description: This report encompasses the final outcomes of a three-year architectural study for Heathrow Terminal 5, to generate guidelines to imporove wayfinding for all inside the airport terminal
findings: No new findings were presented in this report. Instead, it focuses on the consolidation and presentation of the ideologies, issues and potential solutions from the previous two works.
outputs: Interactive CD-rom developed for the client BAA's use, detailing the findings and influences that this project should have on future airport interior spaces. It is structured around a set of Wayfinding Principles for designers/architects to follow.

title: Optare alero CSV: a service delivery vehicle for excluded communities
author: Owen Evans
description: This project investigates applications for the Optare Alero vehicle, exploring modular and adaptable interior configurations to facilitate use by a diverse range of public and professional groups.
findings: Potential underserved user needs are diverse and changable, so in creation of a vehicle that can be suited to a wide range of underserved users, considerations such as modularity and adaptability are key.
outputs: Final concept which incorporates modular seating arangements, adaptable space configurations, and additional trailers to extend functionality.

title: Perception, presence, prediction: intelligent vehicle services that address user needs
author: Edward Goodwin; Richard Hartshorn
description: This report describes design applications developed for a new sensor-based technology, aiming to make living and travelling in the city safer and less stressful.
findings: MCM tech is very applicable to vehicles and inner city scenarios, as it enables fast transfer of information, though displaying information without overloading the user is important.
outputs: From a expansive set of concepts, three business models were developed: Helpful Services (in car communications for more detailed navigation and integrations), Emergency services (using additional data to enable fast and accurate responses to emergency situations), and Monitoring services (allowing vehicles to monitor external conditions and respond automatically).

title: Future London Taxi
author: Dale Harrow; Rama et al Gheerawo
description: This study outlined a new approach to designing an inclusive London taxi for people of all ages and abilities.
outputs: Information was made public, many features now exist in current Taxis. Linking back to the research may be difficult.
challenges: Change of CEO and CFO led to project abrupty stopping

title: Real-time travel: navigating the intelligent environment
author: Nick Rawcliffe
description: This study investigates the use of remote sensor technologies in public transport systems to enhance people's personal mobility within city centres.
findings: City centre wayfinding is difficult for a wide range of diverse users, due to high complexity or hard to find transport information. Each person's travel is different and presenting all the transport information creates confusion, so giving the user personalised and real-time routing is the ideal.
outputs: Two future (2005) buisness models for Omron. 'Real-Time Travel' (London), ID Pegs and rings holding user profiles and journey details (help find optimum routes). Transport Gates automatically deduct payment and real time information is shown on information panels. 'Happy Travel' (Tokyo) mobile phones store details, interact with ticket gates and provide up to date info.

title: InterchangABLE: new design elements to reclaim the transport interchange
author: Fiona Scott
description: This study investigates how we can improve interchanges: changes between different types of transport, resulting in proposals based on a single hypothetical interchange site in east London
findings: Interchange spaces suffer from a range of issues, stemming from 6 identified problems: accessability, poor public space, low-density, in-between spaces and poor information.
outputs: Internal interim presentations. Conceptual design changes for Stratford Interchange were developed, each adressing one of the problem sets, e.g. Urban Connector, a multi-level link bridge that combats physical disconnection between transport modes.
